dietEvidence.body: The dentition indicates herbivory. Régent et al. (2024) described the dentition and a possible rhamphotheca-like structure; no gut contents are known.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A small brachiosaurid from an island environment, interpreted as a case of insular dwarfism. The size reduction is supported by a growth series.
summary: A small brachiosaurid from an island environment, interpreted as a case of insular dwarfism. The size reduction is supported by a growth series.

discovery.body: Named by Mateus et al., 2006. The record is known from Süntel Formation, Lower Saxony. Many individuals, including juveniles and adults, from a single locality.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Many individuals, including juveniles and adults, from a single locality.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Süntel Formation, Lower Saxony records the species in the Late Jurassic. The numeric range used here is ≈154–151 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skeleton is miniature for a brachiosaurid but retains the high shoulders and long forelimbs of the group. The sample includes juvenile and adult material, allowing ontogenetic comparison.

anatomy.title: Body plan
anatomy.body: The species is reconstructed as quadrupedal from the preserved limb skeleton. The posture is not observed; the island setting is inferred from the geology.

behaviour.body: The many individuals from one locality show that the species occurred together, but social behaviour is not established. Dwarfism is a body-size pattern, not a behaviour.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from many individuals, including juveniles and adults, from a single locality. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The dwarfism is supported by a growth series and bone histology, but the island context is inferred from sedimentology and palaeogeography. Sander et al. (2006) diagnosed insular dwarfism from histology; later work described the axial, cranial and appendicular skeleton. The phylogenetic position within Macronaria is debated.
